summary: A Chinese command is the plain verb — it never changes its form: 来！ ‘come!’, 等我！ ‘wait for me!’, 进来！ ‘come in!’. The subject 你 / 你们 may stay (你来！ is a firm ‘YOU come’). Small words set the tone: 请 before the verb makes it polite (请进 ‘please come in’, 请坐 ‘please sit down’), 吧 at the end makes it a suggestion or a friendly push (我们走吧 ‘let’s go’, 你来吧 ‘do come’), and ‘don’t’ is 别 or 不要 before the verb (别走！ ‘don’t go!’, 不要开车 ‘don’t drive’). There is no singular / plural or formal / informal form of the verb: politeness comes from 请, 您 and 吧, number from 你 / 你们.

head: Tone
Chinese
Meaning
rows: Come! Wait for me! Come in!
YOU come! You (all) wait for me!
请进！ 请坐！ 请等我。
Please come in! Please sit down! Please wait for me.
Would you please wait a moment.
我们走吧！ 你来吧！ 坐出租车吧！
Let’s go! Do come! Take a taxi!
Don’t go! Don’t wait for me.
不要开车！ 请不要在这里等。
Don’t drive! Please don’t wait here.
blocks.caption: Commands: the verb stays the same, the small words change

blocks.title: No imperative form — compare German
blocks.text: German komm / kommt / kommen Sie changes the verb for one person, several, or politeness. Chinese keeps 来 for all of them: 来！ 你们来！ 请您来！

blocks.title: 请 goes first
blocks.text: 请 stands before the verb, never at the end of the request: 请等我, not *等我请.

items.title: 不 — not (a statement)
points: 我不开车。 I don’t drive.

blocks.title: 吧 makes it friendly
blocks.text: A bare 走！ can sound brusque; 走吧！ is ‘come on, let’s go’. With 我们 it is ‘let’s’: 我们坐出租车吧. With 你 it is a gentle push: 你先吃吧 ‘go ahead and eat’.

blocks.title: Signs and notices
blocks.text: Written commands use 请 and 请勿 ‘please do not’: 请勿吸烟 ‘no smoking’, 请排队 ‘please queue’.

askYourself: Is it a command or a request? → the plain verb, unchanged.
Do I want to be polite? → put 请 before the verb (请您 … for very polite).
Is it a suggestion, ‘let’s …’, or a friendly push? → add 吧 at the end (我们 … 吧 for ‘let’s’).
Is it ‘don’t …’? → 别 + verb (spoken) or 不要 + verb; not 不 alone.
Am I singling out the person? → keep 你 / 你们 before the verb.
Did I put 请 at the end of the request? → move it before the verb.

traps: *不走！ for ‘don’t go!’ → 别走！ / 不要走！
There is no plural or polite form of the verb (German kommt, kommen Sie): 你们来, 请您来 — the verb is still 来.
吗 turns it into a question, not a command: 你来吗？ ‘are you coming?’ vs 你来吧！ ‘do come!’

quiz.why: A negative command uses 别 (or 不要) before the verb; 不走 is ‘(I’m) not going’.
我们 … 吧 = ‘let’s’; 吗 would make it a question.
The verb does not change; 你们 shows that several people are meant.
吧 makes a friendly suggestion; 你来吗？ would be the question.
请 first, then 不要 + verb.

notes.text: Greek has imperative forms for one and several (έλα / ελάτε) and a separate negative, μην + subjunctive (μην έρθεις); Chinese keeps the verb and adds words: 来！ 你们来！ 别来！
Russian иди / идите change for number and politeness, and не + imperative makes ‘don’t’; Chinese: 去！ 你们去！ 别去！ — the verb never changes. пожалуйста may come last; 请 must come first.
Spanish ven / venid / venga change for person and politeness, and ‘don’t’ uses the subjunctive (no vengas); Chinese keeps 来 and adds 请, 别, 吧.
English already uses the bare verb (Come! Wait!), like 来！ 等！; but ‘please’ can go at the end and ‘don’t’ needs ‘do’ — 请 always comes first, and ‘don’t’ is 别 / 不要. ‘Let’s go’ ~ 我们走吧.
French viens / venez change for tu / vous; Chinese 来 stays for all. ne … pas ~ 别 / 不要 before the verb. s’il vous plaît closes the request; 请 opens it.
German komm / kommt / kommen Sie mark number and politeness on the verb; Chinese marks them with 你们 and 请 / 您. lass uns gehen ~ 我们走吧.
Hindi imperatives change with politeness (आ, आओ, आइए ‘come’), and मत makes ‘don’t’ (मत जाओ); Chinese keeps 来 and shows politeness with 请: 请进. मत ~ 别.
Persian imperatives take be- and a plural / polite -id (boro / beravid ‘go’), and ‘don’t’ is na- (naro); Chinese keeps the bare verb: 去！ 你们去！ 别去！
Marathi imperatives change for politeness and number (ये / या ‘come’); Chinese keeps 来 and adds 请 for politeness.
Arabic imperatives change for gender and number (uktub / uktubī / uktubū ‘write’), and ‘don’t’ is lā + jussive; Chinese keeps the bare verb and adds 别 or 不要.
Hebrew imperatives change for gender and number (bo / bo’i / bo’u ‘come’), and ‘don’t’ is al + future (al tavo); Chinese keeps 来 and adds 别: 别来！
Turkish gel / gelin ‘come’ change for number and politeness, and the negative is a suffix (gelme ‘don’t come’); Chinese keeps 来 and adds 别: 别来！ lütfen may come last; 请 must come first.
Japanese softens commands with verb forms (来てください ‘please come’, 来ないでください ‘please don’t come’); Chinese puts words before an unchanged verb: 请来, 别来. ください follows the verb, 请 precedes it.
Korean commands are verb endings by speech level (오세요, 와), and ‘don’t’ is -지 마세요; Chinese uses 请 / 别 before an unchanged verb and 吧 at the end for ‘let’s’.
Finnish tule / tulkaa change for one or several, and ‘don’t’ is a negative verb (älä tule); Chinese keeps 来 and adds 别: 别来！
Hungarian imperatives have person endings (gyere / gyertek, polite jöjjön ‘come’), and ‘don’t’ is ne (ne gyere); Chinese keeps 来, and 别 does the work of ne.
Swahili uses the bare stem for one person (soma ‘read’) and -ni for several (someni); Chinese keeps the verb and adds 你们. ‘Don’t’ is a si- form (usisome ‘don’t read’); Chinese uses 别.
Luganda uses the bare stem for one person (genda ‘go’) and another form for several; Chinese keeps 去 for all and adds 你们 when needed.
Vietnamese commands work like Chinese ones: the bare verb, mời / xin before it ~ 请, đừng ~ 别, and đi / nhé at the end ~ 吧 (ăn đi! ‘eat!’).
Inuktitut has imperative endings for one, two and several people; Chinese keeps the verb unchanged and adds 你 or 你们 if needed.

seeAlso.note: German has three imperatives (komm! / kommt! / kommen Sie!) and puts the verb first; Chinese keeps the bare verb for everyone and adds 请 for politeness, 吧 for a suggestion, 别 / 不要 for ‘don’t’ (Geh nicht! = 别走！).
Arabic builds the imperative from the jussive and marks gender and number (اِذْهَبْ، اِذْهَبِي، اِذْهَبُوا); ‘don’t’ is لَا + jussive (لَا تَذْهَبْ). Chinese marks none of this: 去！ 别去！
Hebrew has imperative forms for him, her and them (לֵךְ, לְכִי, לְכוּ), and speech often uses the future instead (תֵּלֵךְ); ‘don’t’ is אַל + future (אַל תֵּלֵךְ). Chinese: 走！ 别走！
不 and 没 (S08) negate statements; commands take 别 / 不要.
